documents.abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly being explored as clinical decision-support tools in dentistry.Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) plays a vital role in implant site assessment and prosthodontic treatment planning; however, interpretation of CBCT data requires clinical expertise and may vary among clinicians.The reliability and accuracy of AI chatbots in CBCT-based implant planning remain insufficiently explored.Aim To evaluate and compare the accuracy and reliability of an AI chatbot in CBCT-based implant site assessment and prosthodontic treatment planning with expert prosthodontist evaluations. Materials and MethodsTwenty CBCT cases indicated for single-tooth implant placement were selected from departmental archives.Each case was independently evaluated by an AI chatbot (ChatGPT) and expert prosthodontists with a minimum of five years of clinical experience.Standardized clinical scenarios and a predefined set of ten structured questions related to implant site assessment and treatment planning were used for all evaluations.Expert consensus responses served as the reference standard.AI-generated responses were scored using a three-point ordinal scale: 0 = incorrect, 1 = partially correct/incomplete, and 2 = completely correct.Descriptive statistics and Chi-square analysis were performed, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. ResultsThe AI chatbot demonstrated higher accuracy in implant site suitability assessment and identification of critical anatomical structures, with accuracy percentages of 94.7% and 92.5%, respectively.Moderate accuracy was observed for bone assessment, implant angulation, implant positioning, and prosthodontic treatment planning.The lowest accuracy was observed for implant length and diameter selection (60.0%).The overall weighted accuracy of the AI chatbot was 79.6%.Chi-square analysis demonstrated a statistically significant difference in response distribution among evaluated parameters (χ² = 51.62,df = 18, p < 0.001).Conclusion AI chatbots demonstrated acceptable overall accuracy in CBCT-based implant site assessment and prosthodontic treatment planning, particularly in basic diagnostic and anatomical evaluation tasks.However, reduced accuracy was observed in complex treatment planning decisions requiring advanced clinical judgment.AI chatbots may serve as useful adjunctive tools in implant dentistry and prosthodontics but cannot currently replace expert clinician evaluation.Further studies with larger sample sizes and multiple AI platforms are recommended.

documents.abstract: Background Spirometry is one of the most used pulmonary function tests for assessing respiratory function and diagnosing ventilatory disorders in clinical practice. Evaluation of test validity and interpretation is typically performed by trained healthcare professionals. The present study aims to evaluate the capability of a publicly available large language model (LLM) to perform quality assurance and interpretations of spirometry tests. Methods A total of 150 spirometry tests were retrospectively collected from the pulmonary function laboratories. The spirometry tests were evaluated for acceptability and interpreted by clinicians according to ATS/ERS recommendations as part of standard clinical practice. Subsequently, a publicly available LLM (ChatGPT 5.5) was prompted to evaluate the acceptability and interpret the same spirometry tests according to ATS/ERS criteria. The model interpreted each spirometry test on three separate occasions for assessing reproducibility. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), were calculated by comparing LLM assessments with clinician assessments of spirometry test acceptability and interpretation. Results For spirometry acceptability evaluation, ChatGPT demonstrated an overall accuracy of 87% (95% CI: 81%-92%), sensitivity of 91% (95% CI: 85%-95%), specificity of 61% (95% CI 39%-80%), PPV of 94% (95% CI: 89%-97%), and NPV of 48(95% CI: 29%-67%) with Cohen's k of 0.46. The spiromteric interpretation agreement with the clinicians reference standard was moderate, with exact agreement of 0.61 (95% CI: 0.54–0.69) while Cohen's Kappa (Unweighted) was 0.47 (95% CI: 0.37–0.56) and Macro F1 score was 0.39 (95% CI: 0.33–0.49). Reproducibility across three independent trials was moderate (Fleiss’ κ 0.58). Class-specific interpretation performance varied by category; sensitivity was highest for normal pattern and restrictive defects (0.72), whereas sensitivity for obstructive defects was 0.27. F1-scores were highest for normal and restrictive defects (0.81 and 0.62, respectively). Conclusion The current findings suggest that ChatGPT 5.5 has a limited capability, at its current stage of development, to serve as a reliable tool for independent spirometry interpretation in clinical practice. Nevertheless, it may serve as an adjunct to clinical decision-making and educational tools. Prospective controlled studies are needed to confirm these findings.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Data on the reproducibility, shared error patterns, and multi-year performance of large language models (LLMs) on national orthopaedic board examinations are limited. This study compared the accuracy, response reproducibility, explanation quality, and inter-model concordance of ChatGPT and Gemini on text-based questions from the Turkish Orthopaedics and Traumatology Board Examination (TOTBE), with exploratory benchmarking against published examination statistics. Methods Of 500 TOTBE questions administered between 2021 and 2025, 52 image-based and one annulled question were excluded, leaving 447 text-based questions. Each question, presented in its original Turkish language, was submitted twice to ChatGPT 5.2 (OpenAI) and Gemini 3 Flash (Google) via their public interfaces on January 20 and January 27, 2026, yielding 1,788 responses. Primary analyses used the first response at the question level; second responses served for reproducibility assessment and an additional sensitivity analysis, and a generalized estimating equation (GEE) model accounted for within-question correlation. Accuracy was compared using the exact McNemar test. Two orthopaedic surgeons independently rated explanation quality on a 5-point Likert scale (inter-rater reliability, ICC(2,1)). Results ChatGPT answered 377 of 447 questions correctly (84.34%; 95% CI, 80.68–87.41) and Gemini 396 of 447 (88.59%; 95% CI, 85.31–91.21); Gemini was significantly more accurate ( p = 0.011). Reproducibility was excellent for both models (ChatGPT 94.41%, κ = 0.930; Gemini 97.32%, κ = 0.966). Of 35 questions missed by both models, 25 (71.4%) involved the same incorrect option. The GEE analysis confirmed higher odds of a correct response for Gemini (OR, 1.44; 95% CI, 1.10–1.89; p = 0.008). Explanation quality did not differ significantly ( p = 0.065). Both models exceeded the published passing thresholds in every year. Conclusions Contemporary LLMs achieved high accuracy and excellent reproducibility on text-based TOTBE questions, with Gemini demonstrating significantly higher first-attempt accuracy than ChatGPT. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate accuracy, reproducibility, and inter-model concordance together across multiple years of a national orthopaedic board examination. Because only the text-based component was evaluated under non-equivalent testing conditions, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of overall orthopaedic competence or as direct comparisons with human examinees. Clinical trial number Not applicable. Level of evidence Level IV Diagnostic/Methodological Study (retrospective).
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Understanding why people travel is fundamental to activity-based travel demand modelling and transport policy analysis. However, conventional trip purpose inference methods typically represent mobility contexts using predefined numerical or categorical features, which may discard semantic information contained in raw contextual data, thereby limiting their ability to represent and distinguish diverse travel-related contexts. To address this gap, this study proposes TripPurpose LLM, a domain-informed trip purpose inference framework based on large language models (LLMs). The framework integrates traveller attributes, departure time, transport mode, and semantic information from nearby points of interest (POIs) into a unified textual representation, incorporates transport domain knowledge through structured chain-of-thought (CoT) guidance, and adapts pretrained LLMs using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning. Experiments used 10,513 survey-based trip records from Guangzhou, China. Within the TripPurpose LLM framework, retaining the original POI names increased the accuracy of Qwen3-8B from 0.695 to 0.745 and its Macro-F1 from 0.610 to 0.681, with both metrics exceeding those of structured-feature machine-learning baselines and classifiers using term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features or fixed MacBERT embeddings. This finding highlights the value of contextual semantic modelling for trip purpose inference. Across ten LLM backbones, TripPurpose LLM combining LoRA fine-tuning with CoT guidance consistently achieved the strongest performance among the evaluated settings, with accuracy ranging from 0.71 to 0.76. This pattern demonstrates the framework's effectiveness across different model families and parameter scales. This study provides an integrative framework for inferring trip purposes from travel records, thereby supporting travel-demand analysis, transport planning, and policy evaluation.

Background Brain imaging is central to the structural, functional, metabolic, and neurophysiological characterization of neurological disease, yet interpretation remains constrained by heterogeneity in acquisition, annotation, expertise, and clinical context. Objective This systematic literature review evaluates recent artificial intelligence approaches for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis, with emphasis on methods, modalities, neurological diseases, diagnostic tasks, datasets, validation practices, and translational limitations. Methods The review followed PRISMA 2020 and covered peer-reviewed English-language studies published from January 2020 through June 2026. Eight information sources were searched using database-specific terms for artificial intelligence, neuroimaging, neurological disease, and diagnostic analysis. The search identified 1,078 records; 236 duplicates were removed, 842 unique records were screened, 258 full texts were assessed, and 123 studies were included after a record-level eligibility re-audit. Heterogeneous evidence was synthesized narratively and by descriptive mapping rather than meta-analysis. Results MRI was frequently represented in the included studies and auxiliary mapping data; CT was commonly used in acute stroke and intracranial hemorrhage; PET supported selected molecular and differential-diagnosis studies; fMRI and diffusion imaging were used for network and white-matter analysis; and EEG extended the scope to neurophysiological diagnosis. CNN and three-dimensional networks were commonly reported, while attention, Transformer, graph, self-supervised, generative, multimodal, and foundation-model approaches appeared in selected recent studies. Stroke, dementia, and brain tumors were frequently represented, but heterogeneous populations, outcomes, and incomplete validation extraction precluded ranking diseases, modalities, architectures, or validation strategies. Conclusion The evidence suggests movement from task-specific pattern recognition toward multimodal and context-rich decision support in selected settings, but it does not establish uniform methodological superiority or clinical maturity. Dependable translation requires patient-level data governance, transparent reporting, uncertainty estimation, independent multicenter testing, prospective workflow evaluation, and clinically meaningful endpoints.

documents.abstract: Locoregional therapies are used across the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treatment spectrum, including for curative treatment of small tumors, as bridging or downstaging therapy before liver transplant, for treatment of intermediate-stage disease, and as part of combination treatment with systemic therapy in selected patients. This narrative review summarizes recent developments in transarterial radioembolization (TARE), transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), and percutaneous ablation techniques and separates established clinical advances from early investigational work. The strongest evidence supports personalized TARE dosimetry and radiation segmentectomy, selective TACE with reassessment before repeat treatment, and image-guided thermal ablation with objective margin assessment. Phase 3 trials of TACE combined with antiangiogenic and immune checkpoint therapy demonstrated improved progression-free survival in selected patients with unresectable, nonmetastatic HCC, although the survival benefit of these combinations so far extends only to progression-free survival, and the best treatment sequence remains to be defined. Histotripsy, pulsed electric-field ablation, electrochemotherapy, cryoablation, high-intensity focused ultrasound, imageable or alternative radioembolic microspheres, new embolic agents, robotics, and artificial intelligence remain at different stages of clinical development. Most supporting data are derived from single-arm studies, retrospective cohort studies, trials in mixed liver-tumor populations, or studies in preclinical models. Treatment selection should account for tumor burden and location, liver function, portal hypertension, vascular invasion, transplant candidacy, available alternatives, local expertise, and patient preferences. Future studies should focus on durable local control, preservation of liver function, quality of life, transplant eligibility, overall survival, and cost.

Purpose This study aims to develop a conceptual framework designed to assist organizations in understanding and promoting the adoption of a multidimensional Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO) enterprise risk management (ERM) that integrates artificial intelligence (AI). The proposed framework serves as a tool to improve organizational risk governance, stability, and resilience within an evolving digital landscape characterized by increasingly complex, rapidly changing, and interdependent risks. Design/methodology/approach This study creates a conceptual framework by expanding upon the conventional technology-organization-environment (TOE) model through theoretical integration and tailored ERM contextualization. The methodology includes an extensive review and synthesis of literature on COSO ERM, multidimensional risk perspectives, AI-driven risk management, and technology adoption frameworks. Findings This paper conceptually extends the TOE framework by maintaining its core dimensions while introducing two novel ERM-specific constructs: security and privacy (SnP) and organizational multidimensional risk–technology awareness (ORTA). It also reconceptualizes three existing TOE constructs to better align with COSO ERM realities: organizational compatibility is embedded within organizational readiness (ORD), top management support is operationalized as tone at the top (TtT), and cost is reframed as value for money (VfM). These additions and refinements enhance the explanatory power of the original TOE framework by demonstrating how both traditional and ERM-specific factors shape organizational perceptions of readiness, trust, and strategic alignment in a digital risk environment. Research limitations/implications The proposed framework improves our theoretical understanding of ERM transformation in the digital era by providing a more integrated explanation of how adoption decisions are shaped within complex governance environments. Unlike previous fragmented explanations of technology uptake, this framework demonstrates how interconnected determinants simultaneously influence ERM transformation, especially in AI-enabled settings. Practical implications From a managerial perspective, the framework offers a structured approach for evaluating adoption readiness and designing interventions that facilitate successful COSO ERM transformation. It allows risk leaders to systematically assess internal preparedness across key governance and capability dimensions, with a particular focus on the awareness of multidimensional risk, leadership commitment, and organizational trust in AI-enabled risk systems. Social implications This study has broader societal implications by promoting stronger organizational resilience and more effective risk governance in an increasingly complex and interconnected world. Adopting a multidimensional COSO ERM integrating AI can enhance an organization's ability to anticipate and respond to emerging risks, including financial, operational, cyber, and ESG-related challenges. Originality/value This study addresses an important gap in the literature by investigating the organizational adoption of a multidimensional COSO ERM integrating AI. The interplay between ERM-specific determinants, technological enablers, and managerial adoption intentions in this context remains largely unexplored. By expanding the TOE framework with novel and refined ERM-focused constructs (e.g. ORTA, ORD, VfM, TtT, and SnP), the proposed conceptual model offers a theoretically robust and practically applicable tool for understanding how organizations address strategic, cultural, and governance challenges in digitalized risk management.

This chapter examines the emergence of artificial intelligence–mediated advising in Indian higher education through the lens of digital empathy. It explores how technological systems are reshaping mentorship, accountability, and student well-being, situating India's experience within a comparative global framework. The analysis combines normative critique focusing on rights, ethics, and justice with empirical grounding derived from policy documents, institutional practices, and international case studies. Drawing on theories of care ethics, sociotechnical systems, and the capability approach, the chapter identifies a value–practice gap in current AI deployments. It argues that empathy must be embedded institutionally rather than simulated algorithmically. Comparative evidence from Finland, Singapore, the United Kingdom, and the United States demonstrates that human-centered governance and transparent design foster trust and inclusion.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Machine learning-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) have become critical security infrastructure, but the vast majority of published research reports accuracy only on clean, unperturbed traffic, leaving their robustness to adversarial evasion unexplored. Existing research into adversarial robustness, when it has occurred, has largely imported image-domain approaches of unconstrained perturbation to network traffic, producing "adversarial" examples that could not possibly occur on a real network, and so failing to probe the true robustness of the system to real-world adversaries. We propose AdvRoNIDS, a constraint-aware adversarial robustness framework for NIDS that (i) trains a deep 1D-CNN classifier on flow-based features from the CICIDS2017 benchmark, (ii) crafts adversarial examples using the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) restricted to a feasibility-constrained perturbation set (ПЅ) respecting feature immutability, non-negativity of cumulative counters, and empirical feature bounds, (iii) hardens the classifier through min-max adversarial training against this constrained attacker, and (iv) evaluates the resulting system using a transparent two-number benchmark of clean accuracy and accuracy-under-attack across a full perturbation-budget sweep. The undefended classifier collapses from 90.45% clean accuracy to 25.11% under realistic constrained attack at ε = 0.10, while the adversarially trained classifier retains 87.96% accuracy under the same attack, a 62.85 percentage-point improvement, with negligible cost to clean accuracy (90.45% to 90.86%). A SHAP-based attribution-drift analysis further demonstrates that this robustness arises mechanistically rather than incidentally: the undefended model's decision attribution shifts drastically under attack (mean drift 1.898), while the robust model's attribution remains substantially more stable (mean drift 0.923), a 51.4% reduction that is statistically significant (Mann-Whitney p<1.87×10⁻¹⁶¹,Cliff's δ = 0.70, a large effect). We additionally present an applied explainability and LLM-assisted incident-triage layer that translates the system's outputs into analyst-readable incident narratives. This work explicitly scopes itself to constrained feature-space robustness, leaving end-to-end packet-level attack realizability for future work.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping language learning in higher education, yet students’ engagement in AI-assisted language learning depends on more than access to technological tools. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) as an overarching theoretical perspective, this study examined how emotional intelligence and metacognition were associated with engagement directly and indirectly through enjoyment and self-efficacy, while also evaluating their predictive value. Survey data from 847 university students in China were analyzed using structural equation modeling and random forest analysis with repeated nested cross-validation. The SEM results showed that emotional intelligence and metacognition were positively associated with engagement, enjoyment, and self-efficacy, while enjoyment and self-efficacy were also positively related to engagement. All four indirect effects were significant. The extended random forest model achieved an out-of-sample R² of .472, improving R² by .081 over the baseline random forest and by .069 over the extended linear model. Emotional intelligence showed the highest permutation importance and revealed potentially nonlinear predictive patterns across individual learners. These findings highlight the complementary value of explanatory and predictive approaches for understanding engagement in AI-assisted language learning.

Agentic artificial intelligence extends delegation across networks of human and artificial agents. Research already examines delegated authority, autonomy, trust, accountability and coordination. This article addresses a complementary methodological question: how can agentic delegation, considered as a whole, be governed as a project? Drawing on established project management methodologies, including the Project Management Body of Knowledge, PRINCE2 and ISO 21502, the paper examines the transposition of project initiation, stakeholder identification, scope definition, planning, resource management, risk assessment, monitoring, change control, acceptance and closure. Particular attention is given to delegated autonomy, successive sub-delegations, alignment, semantic continuity and the preservation of governing constraints. The Agentic Delegation Charter is proposed as an adaptation of the conventional project charter, established at initiation as the constitutive reference for the delegation project. The paper advances a conceptual and methodological framework rather than an empirically validated governance model. Its limitations and directions for future evaluation are explicitly identified.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), synthetic media, social bots, and agentic AI are turning information disorder from a content-verification problem into a governance problem for multimedia information ecosystems. Research on fake news, deepfakes, GenAI misuse, and cyber-enabled influence has developed in largely separate streams, and none of these streams offers an integrated governance model for influence activity coordinated through AI-supported workflows. This study develops such a model through a structured evidence synthesis of 35 peer-reviewed sources published between 2019 and 2026, identified through four structured discovery queries and citation chaining and appraised with evidence-type-specific criteria. The synthesis identifies five mechanisms through which AI reshapes information disorder: influence orchestration, ambiguity production, selective persuasion, hybrid human–machine dissemination, and a trust paradox in countermeasures. On this basis, the study defines agentic influence operations as workflow-level risks and organizes them in a twelve-dimension framework that links AI capabilities, content modality, platform infrastructure, data access, evidentiary trust, organizational harm, and governance control points. It also sets out construct boundary conditions, five propositions with explicit evidence status, a managerial control set, and a phased implementation roadmap. Only the proposition on synthetic media and uncertainty about authentic evidence has direct empirical support; the others are offered for testing through simulation, experimental, design-science, and expert-validation studies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The distinction between AI agents and agentic AI is conceptually defensible when it separates an entitythat acts, the properties of its behavior, and the system that enables goal completion. However, theliterature and providers do not establish a universal boundary between two technologies. An agent cancarry out extended processes, and an agentic system can contain a single agent. This article examinesacademic antecedents, contrasts recent taxonomies, and compares terminology used by OpenAI,Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and other providers. It offers an explicitly non-consensus teachingframework and explains why autonomy, agent count, content generation, learning, and authority shouldbe analyzed separately. Keywords: AI; intelligent agents; agentic AI; autonomy; multi-agent systems; language models;governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Why can similarly configured AI agents amplify engagement in some communities yet mainly redirect it in others? We deployed two autonomous AI agents in separate Farcaster channels (January–February 2026) across two incentive phases: Phase 1 with $Degen token rewards and Phase 2 with social recognition through agent follow-backs and mutual-follow encouragement. In /replyors (71 daily replies at baseline, Attention Saturation Ratio 1.17), the difference-in-differences (DiD)-adjusted engagement lift was +228% in Phase 1 and +118% in Phase 2, consistent with engagement amplification, although the seven-day baseline does not establish parallel pre-treatment trends cleanly. In /degen (244 daily replies, ASR 2.17), the channel-level DiD estimate was +18% (p = 0.71) and not statistically distinguishable from zero despite strong topic-level participation. Because the available /degen–/base control is poorly matched on baseline scale and ASR, that comparison is treated as suggestive rather than a clean causal estimate. Phase 1 generated 967 participant reply messages from 61 unique individuals and 101,980 $Degen distributed. Using historical DEGEN/USD closes at the beginning and end of the 9–22 January reward phase as a broad valuation bracket, the aggregate token budget was on the order of US$111–152; this is not a transaction-time weighted valuation. After token removal, participant reply volume within agent-initiated threads fell by approximately 82–90% and Phase 1 participant retention was 27–34%. We introduce the Contextual Amplification Framework (CAF) and Attention Saturation Ratio (ASR) as provisional, exploratory constructs derived from two treated channels. The evidence is consistent with the possibility that pre-existing attention saturation moderates agent effects, but the ASR is not a validated screening rule and requires multi-site replication. The findings carry implications for platform economics, AI governance, and token incentive design.

Abstract This paper examines upper secondary students’ writing with Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) through a post-structural lens. The aim is to explore how authorship can be understood and described in the age of AI. The empirical material consists of three students’ recorded writing sessions and complementary interviews. Through rhizomatic mapping, the recordings are analyzed with Deleuze and Guattari’s notions of assemblage, affect and becoming, further extended through the concept of distributed authorship. The analyses map three dynamic assemblages in which writing and authorship are redistributed across heterogeneous relations. One assemblage foregrounds AI as the primary authorial agent; another enacts reciprocal human-AI co-writing; and a third positions AI as a threat to writing, creativity, and the climate. Writing with GenAI unfolds as a complex relational practice and authorship emerges as distributed between humans and non-humans. This study raises important questions for education to consider in writing instruction and in developing policies for writing with AI, such as questions of equity and ethics.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) virtual streamers are making live‐commerce selling increasingly scalable, yet human explanation and trust remain central to purchase conversion. This paper develops a Stackelberg model of AI co‐host adoption under algorithmic traffic bias. The platform first chooses a transaction commission and an AI‐oriented traffic bias, after which the brand selects AI‐only selling, human‐only selling, or AI‐human co‐host selling. When a human streamer participates, the brand offers a performance commission, and the streamer chooses costly explanation effort. Algorithmic traffic allocation shapes both market exposure and the marginal return to human effort. Greater AI‐oriented traffic bias weakens effort under human‐only selling but strengthens it under AI‐human co‐hosting by enlarging the revenue base for human explanation. Once AI traffic support makes AI‐only selling more profitable than co‐hosting, human effort drops discontinuously to zero. The model identifies when AI co‐hosting complements human streamers, when traffic support instead induces substitution, and why a commission‐driven platform may favor more AI‐oriented exposure than a welfare‐aware benchmark. Extensions with return risk and two‐part contracts clarify how product fit and compensation design affect the value of co‐hosting. Robustness analyses show that the main qualitative results continue to hold under bounded nonlinear traffic allocation, nonlinear demand, and binding contract constraints.

Purpose Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study aims to examine how employees’ artificial intelligence (AI) dependency is associated with burnout in hospitality. It tests the curvilinear nature of this association, the roles of competence and autonomy as need-related pathways and the moderating role of perceived organizational support (POS). Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 375 AI-using hospitality employees in China through a three-wave time-lagged survey. The measurement model was validated using confirmatory factor analysis. Hypotheses were tested using hierarchical regression with quadratic and interaction terms, and conditional indirect effects were examined using a derivative-based approach with delta-method confidence intervals. Findings AI dependency was associated with burnout in a U-shaped pattern with burnout decreasing from low to moderate dependency and increasing at higher dependency. Consistent with SDT AI dependency was associated with competence and autonomy in inverted U-shaped patterns. Competence and autonomy helped account for this curvilinear association with moderate dependency linked to higher competence and autonomy and lower burnout and high dependency linked to the opposite pattern. POS attenuated the negative curvature in these relationships fundamentally altering how AI dependency relates to employees psychological needs at higher AI dependency levels. Research limitations/implications This study extends hospitality technology and employee well-being research by conceptualizing AI dependency as a nonlinear antecedent of burnout and by integrating SDT with POS as a boundary condition. It clarifies when AI-enabled work shifts from supporting psychological needs to undermining them, and offers a mechanism-based explanation of how organizations can preserve employee well-being as AI becomes embedded in hospitality workflows. Originality/value This study advances hospitality AI and employee well-being research by shifting attention from AI use and adoption to employees’ perceived AI dependency. It develops a nonlinear SDT-based framework that explains how AI dependency is linked to burnout through competence and autonomy and identifies POS as a contextual boundary condition in AI-enabled hospitality work.

Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education by changing how students learn and perform academic tasks. Although AI is associated with greater time efficiency and improved academic performance, its broader effects on student productivity and cognitive effort remain insufficiently understood. This study aims to examine how university students associate AI-led productivity gains with less study time, better grades, better understanding of study material, changes in cognitive effort they put into AI-supported task completion and dependency on AI tools. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted an exploratory survey among university students in Hanoi in late 2024 and proposed an empirical model that pools self-reported time efficiency, academic performance, academic self-efficacy, change in cognitive effort and AI dependency as dimensions of student productivity. The authors control for AI use intensity and AI use in collaboration, as well as for some other socio-demographic characteristics. Given the exploratory nature of the study and the relatively small sample, the empirical analysis follows a staged specification strategy when the authors first estimate a parsimonious baseline model and subsequently introduce two sets of background controls sequentially. The authors further estimate an interaction between cognitive effort change and AI dependency, first in a parsimonious specification and subsequently with additional controls. Finally, the authors produce a sensitivity analysis of the model to alternative operationalisation of self-efficacy variable. Findings Students associate their AI-led productivity gains primarily with less study time, a bit less so with better grades and better understanding of the study material. They also associate the productivity growth with greater changes of cognitive effort they put into problem-solving while using AI and rising dependency on AI tools. Self-confidence appears to be associated with likelihood to reap significant rather than some productivity gains particularly once the interaction of AI dependency and AI-led cognitive shift is accounted for. The survey data also support the existence of potentially uneven academic benefits from AI use when higher-achieving students are more likely to report further improvements in academic performance, whereas students with weaker prior performance report rather limited gains. Research limitations/implications The findings highlight the need for research design that captures the dynamic evolution of AI-supported learning. The observed differences between daily and weekly users, particularly in critical evaluation and perceived accuracy, suggest that future studies should examine how evaluative skills and cognitive effort develop over time. Longitudinal and experimental designs, combined with objective performance and AI-usage data, would allow researchers to test whether the productivity dimensions proposed here operate causally or how much the fast-paced evolution of AI tools changes the cognitive effort students put into problem-solving and critical thinking when completing academic tasks, and their dependency on AI tools for academic productivity. Practical implications The results provide actionable guidance for universities seeking to integrate AI into teaching and assessment practices. The strong role of time efficiency and self-efficacy, alongside uneven benefits across student groups, indicates the need for structured AI literacy modules that teach source verification and evaluative strategies and effective prompt formulation. Given that daily users show higher critical evaluation but lower perceived accuracy, teaching practices should incorporate reflective assignments that require students to justify, critique and revise AI-generated content. Assessment formats may need redesign to ensure transparent AI use while still requiring independent reasoning, analytical justification and domain-specific understanding. Social implications Policies should balance the productivity benefits of AI-supported learning with safeguards that promote independent thinking, academic integrity and equitable access. Addressing disparities in AI literacy and access is essential to prevent the widening of the existing academic inequalities. Originality/value This study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-assisted learning by examining students’ perceived productivity gains alongside several concurrent dimensions of their AI-supported academic experience, including time efficiency, perceived academic performance, academic self-efficacy, changes in cognitive effort and AI dependency. Rather than proposing these dimensions as new constructs or causal mechanisms, this study brings them together within a single analytical framework. Particular attention is given to whether perceived productivity gains and growing reliance on AI coexist with self-reported changes in cognitive effort, an interplay that remains insufficiently explored in the existing research. Empirically, this study provides exploratory evidence from Vietnam, an underrepresented higher education context in Southeast Asia.

documents.abstract: Abstract This article examines the state of the art in AI literacy and STEM education and identifies emerging frontiers and research priorities to inspire cutting-edge empirical and theoretical research. The reviewed research is grounded in established AI literacy frameworks and shows that there is potential for students’ development of a critical and technologically informed AI literacy. However, the research is unevenly spread across the STEM disciplines and the potential for AI to transform STEM learning remains unclear. Thus, while the field has expanded rapidly, particularly with the emergence of generative AI (GenAI), fundamental challenges remain. The conceptual ambiguity surrounding AI literacy, combined with the rapid evolution of AI technologies, demands continued theoretical refinement and empirical investigation. Critical questions remain regarding how AI literacy intersects with disciplinary STEM literacies, how GenAI tools both support and reshape teaching and learning processes, and what opportunities and trade-offs arise when students engage with AI as learning partner. The ethical dilemmas of AI integration, including bias, data privacy, and environmental sustainability, also warrant urgent attention. As STEM education increasingly engages with AI as both a subject of learning and a learning tool, future research must move beyond one-size-fits-all frameworks toward context-sensitive approaches that empower educators and learners to critically and responsibly engage with AI while preserving core STEM learning goals. This article highlights key research frontiers and priorities for advancing scholarship at the intersection of AI literacy and STEM education.

Background: Systematic and scoping reviews rely on established frameworks such as PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome), SPIDER (Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation, Research type), and PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) to structure research questions, guide evidence synthesis, and ensure transparent reporting. These frameworks were developed for linear, human-driven workflows involving manual searching, screening, and data extraction. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) and Generative AI (Gen-AI) introduces new capabilities for semi-automated literature discovery, screening, data extraction, and thematic synthesis. However, the methodological implications of AI-assisted evidence synthesis remain underexplored. Methods: This manuscript employed a scoping review–informed methodological analysis of empirical and methodological literature located through structured searches of PubMed and Google Scholar. Preliminary conceptual extensions to PICO, SPIDER, and PRISMA were developed, retrospectively applied to published studies, and independently evaluated by five researchers for applicability, relevance, and clarity. Results: LLMs enable dynamic and iterative processes across evidence synthesis stages, including automated question formulation, large-scale qualitative analysis, and hybrid human–AI screening and extraction. These developments challenge the linear assumptions of PICO, SPIDER, and PRISMA. In response, PICO-AI, SPIDER-AI, and PRISMA-AI incorporate dimensions including prompt transparency, model specification, human-in-the-loop validation, Human–AI workflow classification, data governance, and AI auditability. Independent evaluation showed 80% item agreement, with overall mean relevance and clarity ratings of 3.2/4. Conclusions: LLMs and Gen-AI do not replace systematic review frameworks; rather, they extend them by introducing adaptive, data-driven workflows. Integrating AI into evidence synthesis requires revised methodological guidance to ensure transparency, reproducibility, and rigour. The proposed preliminary extensions provide a model for incorporating machine intelligence into systematic and scoping review practices.

documents.abstract: Introduction Investment advisers increasingly report using artificial intelligence (AI), but little is known about what they disclose about it in fiduciary filings. The SEC brought its first AI-washing enforcement actions in 2024, so regulators and researchers need a reproducible measure of AI disclosure. We provide large-sample evidence on AI disclosure in Form ADV Part 2A brochures and show how the estimate depends on measurement design. Methods We drew a stratified random sample of 400 SEC-registered investment advisers from a population of 16,223 firms, crossing adviser type (private-fund vs. wealth/retail) with 2024 assets-under-management (AUM) quartile. A large language model (LLM) classified the 388 available brochures under a prespecified five-label typology: investment-process use, operational or client-service use, AI-related risk, explicit non-use, and named AI vendors. We treated the LLM as a measurement instrument and validated it three ways: same-family reproducibility, blinded cross-family recoding of 180 brochures, and human verification of 158 cases. Secondary analyses compared brochures with 283 matched firm websites and applied a screen derived from SEC enforcement orders. Results AI use is disclosed in 23.7% of brochures (22.7% survey-weighted), while 27.6% contain AI-related risk language. The within-brochure difference is significant (McNemar p = 0.036). Disclosure rises from 10.4% in the smallest AUM quartile to 43.8% in the largest, and is higher among private-fund advisers. Against human coding, the composite any-use measure achieves precision of 0.76 and sensitivity of 0.81. The same corpus yields estimates of 9.9%, 13.1%, and 23.7% under alternative constructs, adviser universes, and weighting schemes. A literal keyword rule misses or mislabels roughly a quarter of cases. A raw 17.3-percentage-point brochure–website gap disappears after conditioning on document length. None of the five enforcement-screen matches was adjudicated as an unsubstantiated promotional claim. Discussion Advisers present AI at least as often as a risk as a capability, and disclosure is concentrated among larger and private-fund advisers. AI-disclosure prevalence reflects measurement design as much as adviser behavior, so estimates should be reported with their construct, universe, weighting, and validation. The validated framework and an open reproducibility capsule provide a baseline for monitoring AI claims and AI-washing in investment management.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into recruitment, focusing on the underexplored role of AI virtual assistants (AIVA). This study aims to evaluate how AIVA transforms recruitment practices and to provide a systematic research agenda for future applications. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) and a bibliometric analysis (BA) to assess the use of AIVA in recruitment over the past decade, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines. A structured search of the Scopus and Web of Science databases identified 5,301 publications from 2015 to June 1, 2026. After screening, the authors selected 255 papers for full-text review and BA, using R and VOSviewer. They systematically summarized and guided the exploration of current research. Findings The findings suggest that AIVA affects every phase of the recruitment process, from identifying staffing requirements to onboarding new personnel, with publications increasing significantly after 2023. The thematic analysis identified four key themes: isolated mature areas, innovation drivers, transitional uncertainties and broad foundational concepts. In addition, this SLR and BA critically examined the existing literature, highlighting advances and identifying gaps for future research. It also proposed a research agenda to guide subsequent investigations. Research limitations/implications This study is limited to publications indexed in Scopus and Web of Science, which potentially excludes relevant literature. Future research should expand to diverse data sets and explore the longitudinal impacts of AIVA adoption. Practical implications The findings provide actionable pathways for Human Resources (HR) practitioners to integrate AIVA into recruitment, thereby improving decision-making and reducing inefficiencies. Social implications AIVA adoption may improve recruitment equity, fairness, inclusivity and efficiency. Originality/value This paper uniquely synthesizes recruitment literature on AIVA through a dual SLR and BA approach. It advances theory by operationalizing broad AI research directions into domain-specific insights and offers practical implications for reducing recruitment costs, enhancing efficiency and guiding stakeholders in adopting AIVA.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Background The registry record of psychedelic and related rapid-acting compounds is large, heterogeneous and laborious to synthesize by hand. We tested whether a large language model (LLM) with live access to the ClinicalTrials.gov application programming interface (API) could produce a timely, structured and reproducible characterization of this landscape. Methods Cross-sectional analysis of interventional trials on ClinicalTrials.gov as of 13 January 2026. The core-set comprised classic serotonin 5-HT2A agonists, MDMA, ibogaine and ayahuasca; ketamine and esketamine in psychiatric indications formed a separately reported comparator class. Claude (Anthropic), connected to the registry API, retrieved records first through open-ended natural-language querying and then through a documented protocol of field-specific query expressions restricted to records first posted by the search date, which yielded every reported count; populations and indications were defined from structured registry fields. Results Excluding withdrawn records, 412 core-set trials were identified (256 in patients), plus 300 ketamine/esketamine trials. Psilocybin accounted for 244 (59%; 181 in patients), MDMA 99 (47), LSD 39 (13), DMT/5-MeO-DMT 36 (12), ayahuasca 6 and ibogaine 4. Depression led for psilocybin (74 of 181 patient trials) and the ketamine class (237 of 300), PTSD for MDMA (35 of 47) and anxiety for LSD (6 of 13). Of 63 phase 2/3 psilocybin trials in depression, 35 (56%) had a depression rating scale as primary endpoint, most often the MADRS (25), 34 (54%) assessed it at weeks 3–6, 26 (41%) excluded adults over 65 and none enrolled adolescents. Twenty-four core-set trials were registered as phase 3, 13 of psilocybin; psilocybin phase 3 programmes plan more than 1900 participants, the pivotal MDMA trials enrolled 100 and 121, LSD phase 3 trials plan 149–245, and no other psychedelic had a phase 3 trial. Five patient trials (2%) had a site in a low- or middle-income country. Conclusions LLM-mediated registry querying yielded a structured, reproducible characterization of a fast-moving field, but only once each count was tied to an explicit, archived query expression; open-ended conversational querying had underestimated the record several-fold for some compounds. The approach complements rather than replaces systematic review, and its accuracy against manual extraction remains to be quantified.

Background/Objectives: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of conditions characterized by alterations in brain development and function, frequently associated with complex genetic architectures. The widespread implementation of next-generation sequencing, particularly whole-exome sequencing (WES), has substantially increased the identification of potentially disease-associated variants, shifting the major challenge from variant detection to their interpretation and prioritization. This review examines the emerging contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) to WES variant interpretation in NDDs, with particular emphasis on AI-assisted variant prioritization and protein structural modelling. Methods: We reviewed conventional computational and emerging AI-driven approaches applicable to different stages of WES interpretation, including variant pathogenicity and functional-effect prediction, evolutionary conservation, splicing assessment, phenotype-informed prioritization, and protein structure prediction. Their methodological principles, applications, and major limitations were critically examined within the context of neurodevelopmental genomics. Results: AI and machine-learning approaches increasingly integrate genomic, phenotypic, functional, and structural information, supporting phenotype-aware candidate prioritization and molecular contextualization of selected variants. However, computational outputs are affected by model-specific limitations and should not be considered independent evidence of pathogenicity. Their added value depends primarily on the complementarity and biological relevance of the information provided, rather than on predictor concordance alone. Conclusions: This narrative review highlights that AI-assisted WES interpretation should prioritize complementary, mechanism-relevant evidence over computational concordance. AI-assisted tools should therefore be selected according to variant class and disease mechanism and integrated with independent clinical, genetic, and functional evidence.

documents.abstract: LLMs are increasingly being embedded into a variety of distributed agentic systems, in the form of agents with APIs, microservices, workflows, and external tools for task completion. Systems need to be able to handle requests that are worded differently but mean the same thing, to make sure routing is consistent, caching can be reused, latency is reduced, reliability is ensured, and governance is supported. Conventional intent representations, beyond simply conveying what users want with their intent and respective slots, do not encode information about user authorization, policies with implications for execution, side effects of actions, locality of execution, and operational implications of intents. Prior work has provided frameworks for normalization, capability discovery and routing in distributed agentic systems, but all this work is done independently and thus does not provide a unified pipeline for handling requests in distributed systems. The main contribution of this paper is to propose a unified framework describing the normalization, discovery, routing, execution control and runtime feedback in distributed agentic systems. The core of this work is the introduction of a canonical representation of intent, called an intent record, which can convey all kinds of semantic information, as well as context, policy, and operational information about the system as a whole, including its uncertainty, to be used by the system’s routing layer. We also introduce a new constraint-first multi-criteria routing process. A reference architecture is also given for such sorts of systems. The architecture’s main functional components are semantic control and its decoupled, cross-governance-deterministic execution. An evaluation framework for the proposed approach in the future is also presented. This framework is not validated through implementation or benchmarking experiments. Such an empirical evaluation is left for future work.

The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) continuously opens up new possibilities in film post-production, including the subsequent relighting of moving images. As a systematic assessment from a film-design and professional-practice perspective has been lacking, this study examines the potentials, limitations, and implications of current AI-based relighting workflows for cinematographic practice. Methodologically, the study follows a qualitative-exploratory research design within practice-based and practice-led frameworks. Three current AI-based relighting systems (Nvidia DiffusionRenderer, Beeble Studio, and SwitchX) were tested across five test shots and evaluated using a cinematography-oriented qualitative evaluation scheme focusing on light plausibility, image quality and texture retention, as well as image integrity and temporal stability. These observations were complemented by eight semi-structured expert interviews with professionals from cinematography, lighting, and color grading. Results suggest that AI-based relighting does not currently replace on-set lighting but offers considerable potential as a selective correction and extension tool. Its strengths are particularly evident in wide and establishing shots, where faces and fine image details are less perceptually salient, as well as in situations where the desired lighting conditions are difficult to achieve or maintain on set due to weather, time, or budget constraints. Technical and creative limitations are most apparent in workflow integration and usability, as well as in texture loss and image alterations that impair visual credibility, particularly in portrait shots. The findings suggest the potential for a selective shift of certain lighting decisions toward post-production rather than a general replacement of on-set lighting. To maintain a coherent lighting design when substantial lighting decisions are deferred to post-production, greater continuity of cinematographic expertise and creative agency across production and post-production may be required.

The AI-Based Smart Interview Analyzer System is an artificial intelligence-based web application developed to help students and job seekers improve their interview skills through interactive mock interviews, automated performance evaluation, and personalized feedback. In today’s competitive employment environment, candidates often face challenges such as nervousness, poor communication skills, lack of confidence, and insufficient interview practice. Traditional preparation methods may not provide immediate and consistent feedback, creating a need for an intelligent system that supports effective and personalized interview preparation. The proposed system integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to support interview practice and analyze candidate responses. It provides job-role-based interview preparation, maintains interview history, and helps users identify their strengths and weaknesses through feedback. The application consists of two main modules: the Admin Module and the Student Module. The Admin Module manages student information, job roles, interviews, and feedback, while the Student Module allows users to access their dashboard, practice interviews, review previous sessions, view feedback, and manage their profiles. The system aims to provide an accessible and structured environment for continuous learning and performance improvement. By combining AI-based assessment with a user-friendly web interface, the AI-Based Smart Interview Analyzer System can help candidates develop better communication skills, increase confidence, and improve their readiness for real-world job interviews. Future enhancements may include advanced speech analysis, facial expression recognition, body-language assessment, multilingual support, and more comprehensive real-time performance evaluation

We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI. This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: The instruments used for intraoperative guidance have not improved over the years. Traditional margin evaluations fail in 10–20% of cancer surgeries, and histopathology confirmation can take 48–72 h. A promising alternative is hyperspectral imaging (HSI), which allows for real-time, label-free, non-contact, and detailed biochemical characterization of tissues. This review synthesizes 130 studies from 2015 to 2026, identified through a systematic search across multiple databases following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The studies cover various clinical areas, including surgical oncology (53%), neurosurgery (10.8%), perfusion assessment (6.2%), gastroenterology (5.4%), dermatology (4.6%), and emerging domains (20%). Each clinical area is evaluated using a four-part Translational Readiness Appraisal framework. This framework shifts the focus from technical proficiency to deployment evidence by examining hardware compatibility with operating rooms, real-time workflow integration, cross-site validation, and regulatory readiness. Since 2015, the combination of clinically approved HSI hardware and artificial intelligence has led to a tenfold increase in publications. However, a significant gap remains: none of the reviewed studies meet the evidence criteria necessary for regulatory approval. Of the studies, 48.5% show strong single-site validation, but 50.8% remain in the proof-of-concept stage. The heavy reliance on intra-patient validation tends to inflate performance estimates, leaving issues like calibration across devices and regulatory pathways largely unaddressed. HSI has demonstrated technical maturity in several areas, particularly in head and neck margin assessment and brain tumor delineation. The primary reason for the lack of clinical adoption is not imaging performance but rather the absence of multicenter validation and a formal regulatory evidence framework.
topics: Spectroscopy Techniques in Biomedical and Chemical Research

documents.abstract: The need for precise lithium-ion battery (LiB) monitoring and prognostics has grown significantly with the increasing use of electric vehicles (EVs) and renewable energy system (RES) technologies. State of charge (SOC), state of health (SOH), and remaining useful life (RUL) are three critical performance metrics for ensuring battery safety, functional dependability, and effective energy utilization. Non-linear degradation patterns, operating uncertainties, and dynamic environmental fluctuations are frequently difficult for traditional electrochemical and empirical assessment methods to capture. As a result, recent research has focused on advanced data-driven techniques for comprehensive battery state estimation, notably those based on artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning (DL). This review provides an overview of current methodologies for SOC, SOH, and RUL prediction, with a focus on modern DL architectures such as transformer networks, autoencoder-based latent modeling, neural basis expansion techniques, attention mechanisms, and hybrid optimization-driven frameworks. The article examines new advances in intelligent battery prognostics critically, emphasizing their potential for improved estimation precision, resilience, and flexibility in practical operating scenarios. In addition, it identifies future research directions such as enhanced optimization-assisted frameworks, hybrid physics-informed learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). This article intends to offer a comprehensive overview of modern battery prognostics approaches to aid in the development of dependable, efficient, and long-term battery management system (BMS) solutions for electric mobility and energy storage systems.

Senior High School (SHS) students often face challenges in selecting the most appropriate academic strand due to limited assessment tools and the continued reliance on traditional guidance practices. These methods frequently lack objectivity and comprehensive evaluation, resulting in mismatches between students’ competencies, interests, and their chosen academic pathways. Such misalignment may affect students’ academic performance, educational direction, and future career readiness. This study aimed to develop an AI-Driven Multi-Dimensional Course Assessment and SHS Strand Recommendation System designed to objectively evaluate student competencies and generate strand recommendations that align with learners’ abilities, interests, and career potential. The system intends to support students, teachers, and guidance personnel by providing data-driven insights that can assist in making informed academic decisions. The research employed a quantitative–descriptive design integrated with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). The system was developed using an Input–Process–Output (IPO) conceptual framework combined with Agile Software Development Methodology, enabling iterative system improvement and structured data processing. The platform utilizes a 30-dimension assessment model measuring cognitive skills, literacy and communication abilities, technical aptitude, and personality-interest indicators. Student responses are processed through a structured scoring model and analyzed using an AI-powered evaluation module to generate strand recommendations, competency profiles, and career-related insights, which are presented in a downloadable evaluation report. The results are presented in a comprehensive evaluation report that users can download and use for academic guidance and decision-making. Evaluation results showed strong system performance and user acceptance. Based on the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model, IT experts gave the system an overall mean score of 3.95, indicating a high level of software quality and functionality. System users rated the platform with an overall mean score of 4.00, interpreted as Highly Acceptable, reflecting positive user experience and effectiveness. This finding clearly demonstrates that the system can provide data-driven guidance in SHS strand selection, reduce academic-career mismatches, and support better educational alignment and long-term career readiness among students.

This chapter examines the role of artificial intelligence in advancing personalised disability support within higher education. It analyses key applications, including adaptive learning systems, predictive analytics, and assistive technologies, highlighting their capacity to improve access, engagement, and student success. Attention is given to opportunities for enhancing institutional performance through data-informed decision-making and scalable support systems. Ethical considerations, including transparency, fairness, privacy, and user autonomy, are critically explored, alongside the importance of human-centred and participatory design approaches. The chapter further discusses governance, policy alignment, and capacity building as essential conditions for responsible AI integration. It argues that the transformative potential of AI depends on sustained institutional commitment to inclusive, equitable, and ethically grounded practices.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning models provide powerful data-driven tools for modeling complex nonlinear systems and predicting process behavior from limited experimental data. In this study, an AI-driven predictive framework is developed for modeling paracetamol solubility and solvent density in supercritical carbon dioxide (SC-CO 2 ). A dataset comprising 40 experimental observations was employed, with pressure and temperature used as input variables and paracetamol mole fraction and SC-CO 2 density considered as target outputs. Three machine-learning regression algorithms—Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), Tweedie Regression (TDR), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)—were developed and comparatively evaluated. To enhance predictive performance and automate model configuration, the Cheetah Optimizer (CO), a nature-inspired metaheuristic optimization algorithm, was integrated into the modeling framework for hyperparameter optimization. Model performance was assessed using the coefficient of determination ( R 2 ), mean squared error (MSE), and mean absolute error (MAE). The results demonstrated that TDR provided the highest predictive accuracy for paracetamol mole fraction, achieving an R 2 of 0.985, whereas GPR exhibited the best performance for SC-CO 2 density prediction, with an R 2 of 0.991. The developed framework successfully captured the nonlinear relationships between operating conditions and the predicted properties while demonstrating that the optimal learning algorithm depends on the target variable. These findings highlight the potential of AI-assisted optimization and machine-learning approaches for data-driven prediction and intelligent modeling of complex supercritical-fluid processes.

The current study has been conducted to propose and validate the artificial intelligence (AI)-driven banking ecosystem model for understanding how AI improves customer experience, risk management, and operational efficiency within the context of the banking industry. Specifically, the study aims to overcome the lack of empirical studies providing holistic evidence on how AI works in emerging regional banking markets by analysing the influence of AI awareness, AI application, and AI effectiveness on banking performance. The study utilises quantitative and explanatory research designs and data collection procedures. In total, 480 participants, including customers, employees, and branch managers of scheduled commercial banks have been surveyed. The AI-driven banking ecosystem has been defined using the constructs of AI awareness, AI application, and AI effectiveness. Descriptive statistics, reliability and validity testing, CFA, and SEM have been used for data analysis. The findings show that the AI-driven banking ecosystem positively influences all dimensions of banking performance. In addition, risk management (β = 0.751, p < 0.001), operational efficiency (β = 0.704, p < 0.001), and customer experience (β = 0.582, p < 0.01) had the highest impact on performance in the banking industry. The structural model presented satisfactory goodness-of-fit indicators, which confirmed the conceptual framework of the research and all the hypotheses of the study. In addition, the research suggests the development of an integrated AI driven banking ecosystem framework that takes into account technological, organisational, and strategic aspects of AI.

This chapter delves into the transformative synergy between artificial intelligence (AI) and smart contracts, positioning them as the next frontier in managing digital assets and virtual currencies. It introduces the core concepts, illustrating how AI injects adaptability into rigid blockchain-based contracts, enabling real-time adjustments, predictive analytics, and autonomous dispute resolution. From an economic perspective, the integration drives efficiency in decentralized finance (DeFi), with the total value locked surging to $129 billion by mid-2025, thereby democratizing access while posing risks such as market bubbles. Socially, it promises inclusion for underserved populations through microlending and empowers communities via decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs), yet raises concerns over biases, job disruptions, and digital divides. Policy analysis examines frameworks such as the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) guidelines, balancing innovation with consumer protection in central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) like the Digital Euro and e-CNY. Business perspectives highlight competitive edges in supply chain optimization and tokenized economies, with practical recommendations for risk mitigation. Key applications explored include dynamic contract optimization using machine learning, AI oracles for trustless data integration, and AI-driven DAOs for governance. Institutional and retail use cases demonstrate AI-audited compliance and robo-advisors for portfolios. Regulatory and ethical challenges, including the legal personhood of AI-augmented DAOs and issues of bias, transparency, and accountability, are critically assessed. Future directions envision convergences with the Internet of Things (IoT) and quantum computing, fostering self-sustaining ecosystems amid risks such as encryption vulnerabilities and opportunities for trillions in value creation. Aimed at business professionals, academics, and regulators, the chapter provides actionable insights to navigate and profit from this evolving landscape, emphasizing ethical and sustainable practices.

Semantic communication offers a method for task-oriented information delivery in artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled space networks, but compact semantic representations remain vulnerable to fading, noise, and structured corruption during transmission. This work proposes Clean–Impaired Semantic Preservation for Robust Semantic Communications (CISP-SemCom), a link-level semantic communication framework that explicitly learns from the clean latent representation and its communication-impaired counterpart generated from the same source sample. In a shared projection space, class-aware Clean–Impaired Contrastive Alignment (CI-Con) preserves cross-sample discrimination while excluding same-class non-matched samples from the negative set, and Semantic Preservation (SP) directly promotes consistency within each matched clean–impaired pair. In a ten-seed controlled same-backbone evaluation on CIFAR-10 under Rician fading, CISP-SemCom increases the normalized area under the robustness curve (AURC) evaluated over the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) (SNR-AURC) from 66.85 ± 2.36 to 72.48 ± 1.24, corresponding to a paired gain of 5.63 AURC points with a 95% confidence interval of [3.75, 7.51]. Mechanism diagnostics show that SP-only optimization admits projector collapse, and that class-agnostic contrastive learning introduces same-class false-negative pressure. A direct class-aware ablation further indicates that most of the measured task-robustness gain comes from class-aware CI-Con, while SP acts as an explicit matched-pair consistency regularizer. On EuroSAT RGB, SNR-AURC increases from 65.53 ± 1.80 to 75.35 ± 1.58, showing that the robustness improvement is also observed on a second dataset. Decoder-independent latent probes further show improved accessibility of task-relevant class information, while the measured batch-1 inference latency remains similar to Backbone. These results support clean–impaired semantic preservation as an effective strategy for robust task-oriented transmission under satellite-inspired link impairments.

Background: The “2 Sigma Problem”, where individualized tutoring outperforms conventional instruction by two standard deviations, remains a persistent challenge in large-enrollment pharmacy courses. Generative AI tutors, constrained to instructor-verified content, offer a scalable, equitable approximation of personalized support. Methods: Four course-specific AI tutors were deployed across first-year (P1; n = 108–119/cohort) and third-year (P3; n = 98–108/cohort) Doctor of Pharmacy cohorts (Fall 2024–Spring 2026) using ChatGPT-4o and PlayLab with retrieval-augmented generation. Effectiveness was evaluated through longitudinal grade analysis, American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy proficiency outcomes, satisfaction surveys, and anonymized interaction log analysis. Results: Engagement was heterogeneous across curricular formats: 15-week P1 courses supported sustained weekly usage for foundational concept reinforcement, whereas 4-week P3 modules exhibited lower, targeted utilization focused on rapid self-assessment. In P1 Biochemistry, tutor integration was associated with longitudinal cohort exam improvements. The overall targeted metabolism exam mean rose from 74.0% (Fall 2023, no AI) to 81.4% (Fall 2024, AI tutor) and 83.6% (Fall 2025, AI tutor), with active users (n = 16, 85%, Fall 2024) outperforming non-users (n = 16, 79.3%, Fall 2024) by 5.7 percentage points, and with higher mean scores observed across progressively higher usage tiers. AACP proficiency means increased from 77.9% to 82.1%, exceeding the 80% benchmark. In P1 Physiology and P3 modules, cohort performance remained consistently high (83.7–88.2%), maintaining AACP benchmark proficiency across all observation cycles. Student perceptions were positive regarding conceptual clarification and adaptive explanations. Conclusions: Curriculum-aligned AI tutors represent a viable strategy for approximating individualized instruction in pharmacy courses. Course-specific AI tutors demonstrate feasibility across PharmD curricula, functioning as continuous retrieval-practice tools in foundational sciences and as targeted self-assessment aids in accelerated modules. Educational benefits and adoption dynamics are moderated by curricular pace, subject complexity, and assessment structures, highlighting key considerations for broader health sciences implementation.
