documents.abstract: Background Low back pain (LBP) is a major occupational health problem among care workers. However, few studies have classified LBP by both severity and chronicity or examined associations of health literacy with presenteeism. This study aimed to assess LBP prevalence, classify LBP by severity and chronicity, and identify the associated physical and psychosocial factors. We conducted a secondary exploratory analysis to examine hypothesized indirect associations between health literacy and presenteeism involving psychological distress and LBP-related disability. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1022 care workers employed at long-term care facilities. Participants were categorized into five groups: non-LBP and four LBP groups defined by severity (non-severe vs. severe) and chronicity (non-chronic vs. chronic). Sociodemographic, work-related, health literacy, and psychosocial factors were analyzed using multinomial logistic regression. The secondary exploratory analysis examined the hypothesized indirect statistical associations using psychological distress and LBP-related disability. Results The prevalence of LBP was 75%. Severity and chronicity were not fully concordant, supporting classification by both dimensions. Unsuitable posture was associated with all LBP groups. Severe LBP was associated with higher psychological distress and greater presenteeism, whereas low health literacy was independently associated with severe chronic LBP. The secondary exploratory analysis identified significant indirect associations of health literacy with presenteeism involving psychological distress and LBP-related disability. Conclusions LBP among care workers is highly prevalent and multifactorial. The factors associated with LBP differed according to severity and chronicity, highlighting the importance of considering both dimensions together with physical and psychosocial factors when assessing LBP among care workers.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Background Chronic benzene (BZ) exposure is a well-established cause of hematological malignancies, but its potential association with immunosenescence-related alterations at occupational exposure levels below current regulatory limits remains unclear. This cross-sectional study investigated the associations of cumulative BZ exposure with genotoxicity, immunosenescence-related, and hematological biomarkers. Methods The study included 228 participants: 115 workers directly involved in BZ production, 75 administrative workers from the same factories without direct involvement in BZ production, and 38 external controls without occupational exposure to industrial solvents. BZ exposure was assessed using personal air monitoring, and cumulative exposure dose (CED) was calculated from airborne BZ concentrations and exposure duration. Genomic damage was evaluated using the cytokinesis-block micronucleus (CBMN) and comet assays. Immunosenescence-related and cellular-stress markers included the CD4/CD8 ratio, CD28 − frequency, p53 expression, γ -H2AX expression, and mitochondrial DNA copy number. Hematological parameters were assessed using peripheral blood cell counts. Spearman correlation analysis and outcome-appropriate generalized linear models were used to evaluate the associations between CED and the investigated biomarkers. Results After full multivariable adjustment, higher CED was associated with greater comet tail intensity (MR = 1.0827, p < 0.001) and tail moment (MR = 1.0922, p < 0.001) and with lower CD4/CD8 ratio (MR = 0.9743, p < 0.001) and p53 expression (MR = 0.9739, p < 0.001). CED was associated with higher micronucleus frequency (MNF) in the age- and sex-adjusted model (RR = 1.0137, p = 0.033). After further adjustment for BMI, hypertension, smoking status, and alcohol use, the effect estimate remained positive, but the association did not reach conventional statistical significance (RR = 1.0123, p = 0.053). No statistically significant associations were observed between CED and comet tail length, CD28 − frequency, γ -H2AX expression, mitochondrial DNA copy number, WBC, RBC, platelet count, or neutrophil count in the fully adjusted models. Conclusion Cumulative occupational BZ exposure below the applicable regulatory limits was associated with increased comet-assessed DNA damage and selected immune-related alterations, particularly lower CD4/CD8 ratio and p53 expression. The association between CED and MNF remained positive but was not statistically significant after full adjustment. These findings suggest a selective pattern of BZ-associated genotoxic and immune-related alterations rather than generalized hematological toxicity or a uniform immunosenescence phenotype. Prospective studies are needed to determine their long-term clinical and occupational health significance.

documents.abstract: This article aims to analyze the practical application of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies as a transformative factor for the human resource potential of the Supreme Audit Institution (SAI). The study focuses on the audit of the effectiveness of state support within the small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) sector of the Republic of Kazakhstan. The integration of AI algorithms into SAI activities fundamentally redefines the role of the state auditor, transforming them into a data analyst capable of identifying latent correlations between state support volumes and the qualitative growth of the enterprise sector. The study reveals a critical discrepancy: while there is a formal increase in the number of SMEs, current financial incentives in low-tech sectors remain largely ineffective. The findings suggest that the traditional audit system, lacking advanced data analytics, merely records budget absorption indicators without evaluating their impact on the technological complexity and productivity of the businesses involved. The originality of this research lies in the conceptualization of a fundamentally new model of state audit, in which AI serves as the primary driver of transforming SAI human capital. The practical significance is underscored by the development of algorithmic tools for "smart" monitoring of state support, integrated with national databases. The study justifies a methodology for detecting hidden inefficiency risks by automatically benchmarking allocated funds against SMEs' actual contribution to the country’s economic development.

Urban bridge maintenance is a smart-city governance problem involving uncertain evidence, constrained budgets, and safety-critical actions. We present an auditable closed-loop artificial intelligence architecture separating observations, inferred states, alternatives, decisions, and interventions. Mechanisms are validated in SynthTown, a ground-truth municipality with 50 bridges and 842 components, using hidden-state prediction, multiobjective planning, stakeholder screening, feedback recalibration, and verifier-repair safeguards. A public-data implementation covers 1,733 Utsunomiya bridges and integrates 1,592 persistent scatterer interferometric synthetic aperture radar points, inspection records, three-dimensional maintenance models, and capacity-aware plans. Verification eliminated unsafe outputs in the synthetic benchmark.

documents.abstract: The increasing availability of generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems has expanded the possibilities for developing personalized, context-sensitive forms of human–AI collaboration. The effectiveness of such collaborations depends not only on the capabilities of the underlying language model but also on the organization of interaction, the management of contextual information, the consistency of operational rules, the verification of outputs and the allocation of decision-making authority. This paper presents Aureliano, an experimental Human–AI Hybrid Hub (HAHH) framework designed to structure these dimensions within an existing generative AI environment. Rather than introducing a new foundational model, Aureliano operates as a higher-level cognitive and procedural framework that organizes the interaction between a human principal and a general-purpose AI system. Its central objectives are to improve contextual continuity, mitigate semantic drift and entropy, distinguish evidence from inference, support complex reasoning, maintain decision traceability and preserve human authority over consequential decisions. The framework is examined through a conceptual architecture, an operational state-management model, a structured epistemic classification scheme, a human-in-the-loop validation mechanism and an exploratory verification approach. Particular attention is devoted to the distinction between persistent information and autonomous memory, between behavioral consistency and model identity and between internally reported test results and independently reproducible empirical evidence. The analysis suggests that a substantial part of the practical value of personalized AI collaboration may be produced by the systematic organization of the human–AI interface rather than by modifications to the underlying model. Nevertheless, this proposition requires controlled empirical evaluation. The paper therefore distinguishes the framework's specified properties, reported experimental observations and unresolved hypotheses. The contribution is a transferable conceptual approach to the design and evaluation of human-controlled, context-aware AI collaboration, with implications for decision support, knowledge management, organizational analysis and responsible AI governance.

documents.abstract: This archival technical report documents a five-pull-request QSOL-IBAE engineering mission comprising a defensive v0.5 prerequisite and v0.6A-v0.6D. It separates independently checked GitHub merge/release identities from mission-report attestations, offline synthetic conformance and a newly constructed finite executable recovery model. The bounded abstract checker exhaustively explores 3,240 reachable states and 7,289 transitions while checking eight selected recovery/effect safety properties. The case reports a reviewer-attribution correction, an authorization-aware GitHub publication interruption and a native-extension verification restart. It does not claim source-code-level mathematical verification, universal agent reliability, live OpenAI/GitHub activation, external ChatGPT/Work/Codex session reactivation or remote attestation. Includes PDF, Markdown manuscript, original source report, machine-readable evidence ledger, formal specification, executable bounded checker, verification results, citation metadata and SHA-256 checksums.

documents.abstract: Timely forecasting of infectious disease activity supports outbreak alerts, vaccination scheduling and resource allocation in public health surveillance. Modern deep-learning models can be accurate but typically require disease-specific training data and tuning, conditions often unavailable for rare or newly notified pathogens or in settings with limited computational resources. Time series foundation models (TSFMs), pre-trained on large heterogeneous corpora and deployable in a zero-shot manner, offer a candidate solution, but their value for routine multi-disease surveillance has not been systematically assessed. We assembled 289 disease–country time series across over 70 notifiable infectious diseases from six national surveillance systems (China, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Ireland and the United States; 106,234 weekly or monthly observations). Four TSFMs (TimesFM, Moirai, Chronos and TimeMoE; 14–314 million parameters) were evaluated in zero-shot mode and compared with five neural network baselines (DLinear, LSTM, PatchTST, TimeMixer and TimesNet) across one-step-ahead, medium-term and long-term horizons. Forecasts were assessed using MAE, RMSE, MASE and R²; prediction intervals from Moirai variants were additionally compared using the Winkler score. Across 36 settings (6 countries × 3 horizons × 2 metrics, MAE and RMSE), a TSFM variant achieved the lowest observed error in 30 (83.3%). This is a descriptive ranking summary rather than evidence of statistical superiority. The pattern was most consistent at the one-step-ahead horizon, where a TSFM variant ranked first in every country on both metrics, and TSFM variants also ranked highest on MASE and R². Errors did not decrease monotonically with model size in Moirai, Chronos or TimeMoE, and the Moirai variant with the lowest Winkler score varied by country and forecasting horizon. An exploratory multivariate analysis using Moirai indicated that jointly forecasting co-circulating respiratory pathogens may yield additional performance gains. Within the evaluated test periods of this multi-country study, zero-shot TSFMs were competitive with task-specific neural forecasting models trained with fixed default configurations. Because each series was evaluated over a single held-out year, these results do not establish consistent performance across years, epidemic cycles or changing surveillance conditions. Pre-trained TSFMs, particularly small variants that run on modest hardware, are nonetheless a promising starting point for surveillance forecasting pipelines.

Digitization of the United States healthcare system has increased the use of the electronic health records as well as improved the data systems, but smooth data exchange is still a challenge. Although the interoperability standards like Health Level Seven and Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources have been adopted, healthcare data remain fragmented among institutions limiting care coordination and data-driven decision-making. This work provides an assessment of the shortcomings of the existing interoperability strategies and offers a method of health information exchange that is governance-based and scalable and incorporates technical, organizational and policy aspects. The review indicates that even though interoperability standards allow data exchange in a structured and application programming interface format, their success is limited to inconsistent implementation, poor enforcement, and limited practical integration. The institutional silos, inconsistencies in regulations, distrust, and misaligned incentives have continued to cause fragmentation. The review pinpoints the key missing factor in governance, which is roles of policy harmonization, frameworks of trust, and alignment of incentives. It also points out that new technologic systems like federated systems, cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and blockchain can improve scalability when they are backed up by robust governance systems.

Artificial intelligence-assisted computer-aided detection (CAD) can expand access to chest radiography interpretation for pulmonary tuberculosis screening and triage, but high overall discrimination does not ensure safety at a deployed threshold. This focused narrative Mini Review synthesizes evidence on subgroup performance, threshold calibration, external validity, and implementation of CAD for adult pulmonary tuberculosis. Smear-negative, asymptomatic, and some HIV-associated disease may be less radiographically visible, increasing false-negative risk. Conversely, previous tuberculosis and competing chronic abnormalities reduce specificity and concentrate unnecessary confirmatory testing. Sex, age, geography, clinical setting, verification design, and software version can further alter operating performance. A numerical threshold is therefore not a portable algorithm property but a context-specific clinical resource-allocation policy. We propose a lifecycle in which programs define the intended use, lock the product and version, conduct representative local validation, select an operating point under explicit sensitivity and capacity constraints, audit clinically relevant subgroups, and monitor the complete care pathway. Stratified thresholds and multivariable models may improve selected settings, but current evidence does not justify replacing robust local calibration and governance. Prospective evaluations should compare threshold strategies under common verification standards and report missed cases, referral burden, treatment initiation, and patient-important outcomes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become an important part of modern e-commerce, supporting product recommendations, search ranking, customer-review analysis, and personalized shopping experiences. Despite these benefits, customers often receive recommendations without understanding the reasons behind them. This lack of transparency can make it difficult to distinguish a genuinely relevant suggestion from one influenced by popularity, incomplete information, or commercial priorities. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) offers a way to make these decisions more understandable. However, explanations are useful only when they communicate relevant evidence accurately rather than simply presenting convincing language. This paper examines the relationship between XAI, semantic analysis, and transparent decision-making in e-commerce, with particular attention to research trends during 2024, 2025, and 2026. It proposes a conceptual framework that connects customer preferences, product attributes, review sentiment, recommendation models, and evidence-based explanations. The framework is designed to explain why a product may be relevant, which features support the recommendation, and where conflicting information remains. The paper also discusses explanation faithfulness, customer privacy, review reliability, fairness, and the limitations of language-model-generated explanations. Its contribution is a practical design approach for connecting recommendation decisions with verifiable semantic evidence. Future implementation and user testing are required to determine whether this approach improves customer understanding and decision quality in real shopping environments
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Musculoskeletal disorders MSDs, a major concern in occupational health, are frequent among workers in manufacturing companies. While their origins are multifactorial, professional constraints play a preponderant role in their occurrence. Identifying risk factors is essential for developing preventive actions. Objectives To investigate MSDs in a pastry company and determine their occupational and non-occupational risk factors. Methods We conducted an exhaustive cross-sectional study among workers in a pastry company located in the city of Sfax (Tunisia). Data was collected by a socio-demographic/professional questionnaire. The screening of MSDs was carried out by the Nordic questionnaire. Risk factors were determined by bivariate analysis, and the multivariate explanatory model by logistic regression using R software. Results Our population consisted of 221 employees; the majority were women (90.5%) with a mean age of 34.2 ± 8.5 years. The subjects had mean work-seniority of 10.24 ± 6.9 years. Various occupational constraints were reported: an incorrect spinal posture (94.1%), repetitive movements (69.7%) and prolonged sitting posture (51.1%). MSDs were found in 47.5%, preferentially located in the neck, shoulder and lumbar spine. Bivariate analysis revealed significant association between the presence of MSDs in the last 12 months and advanced age, female gender and work-seniority. In addition, MSDs were associated with working in seated prolonged posture (OR = 2.5[1.5–4.3]). In multivariate analysis, the presence of MSDs was significantly associated with age, work-seniority and prolonged sitting posture. Conclusion The prevalence of MSDs was high among the workers in the pastry company. Recognizing individual and occupational risk factors will help to establish appropriate preventive measures.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Building Digital Finance on a New Foundation: New wine in new skins examines the challenges in transaction processing, analysis, and risk management for financial institutions due to financial contract ambiguity, disparate interpretation of terms across counterparties and banks. The authors explain why the status quo is unsustainable, the purpose of the financial industry, the parameters that define financial contracts, and the advantages of adopting the open-source Algorithmic Contract Types Unified Standard (ACTUS) as a viable solution to mitigate risk and increase systemic productivity. They discuss the role of artificial intelligence in probabilistic and deterministic problem spaces. The potential of tokenization is put in context with the concept of smart financial contracts which, by their design, introduce observability, verifiability, and enforceability. The impact of shared ledger technology (distributed ledger technology [DLT]/blockchain) for financial market participants such as financial institutions and regulators is discussed.

Digital twins (DTs) increasingly leverage artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) pipelines, both to build real-time DTs from high-fidelity simulations and to instantiate them with historical data. However, engineering these pipelines remains largely ad-hoc: pipelines are hard to specify, validate, and reuse, with scarce dedicated tooling. Function+Data Flow (FDF) addresses this by defining a visual domain-specific language (DSL) that represents functions (ML models) explicitly, enabling their composition and reuse. We implemented FDF in DesCartes Builder, an integrated modeling environment supporting FDF-based DT synthesis and validation. In this paper, we report on an empirical user study evaluating whether FDF and DesCartes Builder can make AI-based DT development more accessible and reliable. Participants implemented a representative real-time DT prototype within DesCartes Builder, and we measured perceived usability and feature adequacy through quantitative and qualitative measures. Our results indicate that DesCartes Builder and FDF achieve a good level of usability across a broad range of potential users, and particularly for the intended audience of domain experts. The study additionally surfaces concrete strengths and areas for improvement of both the tool and the underlying FDF framework. Informed by these findings, we propose H-FDF, a Hierarchical extension of FDF supporting iterative and modular pipelines, enabling the formal specification of more complex DT pipelines such as dual training. Our findings suggest that integrated, model-driven platforms are a promising direction to transform AI-based DT engineering into a disciplined modeling practice.

This review examines the forensic applications, advantages, and limitations of key spectroscopic techniques, including Raman, infrared (IR), near-infrared (NIR), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), X-ray fluorescence (XRF), and mass spectrometry, in crime scene and laboratory investigations. These techniques are discussed in the context of analyzing evidence, detecting illicit substances (including biological fluids, explosives, and narcotics), and reconstructing crime scenes. The benefits and limitations of each method are highlighted, along with their potential for enhancing forensic investigations. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) with spectroscopic techniques is also briefly explored, noting their role in improving data analysis and interpretation. Challenges such as sensitivity, specificity, and implementation in field settings are discussed, alongside future directions for advancing spectroscopic applications in forensics. This review aims to provide a balanced overview of spectroscopic techniques in forensic science for researchers, forensic scientists, and law enforcement agencies.
topics: Spectroscopy Techniques in Biomedical and Chemical Research

documents.abstract: Human social interaction is full of episodes of help, and the person giving it and the person receiving it may not interpret the same episode in the same way. Against a background of reports that large language models match or exceed human performance on social reasoning tasks, this study asks whether they reproduce this asymmetry between the two sides. Forty-eight Chinese university students read 24 everyday helping scenarios, each in four situational versions, from either the beneficiary’s or the benefactor’s side, and rated the helper’s willingness, the recipient’s need, the difficulty of helping, and the recipient’s gratitude. The identical Chinese materials were then given to 12 models, the flagship and the light model of three providers based in English-speaking countries and three based in China, with 30 independent runs per text, followed by two further prompt conditions: the same scenarios in English for the six models of the Chinese providers and a stated identity prepended to the prompt for all 12. Bayesian mixed models showed a dissociation. On what the situation called for, the models mostly matched the humans or exceeded them: the contrast between a pressing need and one already met was 1.325 scale points in the humans and 1.159 to 1.825 across models, above the human value in 11 of 12. On which side the episode was judged from, most fell short: the humans rated gratitude 0.756 points higher from the beneficiary’s side, the models 0.047 to 0.727, with 11 of 12 credibly below the human estimate. Only Doubao-2.1-Pro matched the humans on gratitude, and it departed from them on willingness and difficulty. Capability tier ordered the 12, though the contrast did not exclude zero, while the provider’s country did not order them at all. Among the six models of the Chinese providers, writing the scenarios in English raised the effect in five, though not to the human estimate. Likewise, across all 12, stating an identity raised it in 10, by 0.10 on average against a mean shortfall of 0.44, and 11 of 12 still sat below the human estimate. Our results suggest that large language models, at least those surveyed here, read what a situation calls for at a level comparable to human readers, but that they show markedly less sensitivity to perspective, namely to the asymmetry with which benefactors and beneficiaries evaluate one and the same act of help.

Background: Deep learning systems for Gleason grading are developed almost entirely on high-end clinical scanners and on cohorts from a small number of Western institutions, yet deployment increasingly involves other devices and other populations. These two distribution shifts, device and population, are rarely tested together on the same physical slides. The PAR dataset, from Erbil, Iraq, digitizes each biopsy on three scanners and provides three distinct pathologist grades, so it permits both tests at once on a Middle Eastern cohort. A concurrent study by the dataset originators validated a task-specific model and two foundation models on PAR; we complement it by testing an independently developed detect-then-grade pipeline and by separating scanner effects on detection from scanner effects on grading. Methods: We applied one fixed model developed on North American and European material to all 1017 whole-slide images (339 slides from 185 patients, three scanners; 49.6% clinically significant cancer) with no scanner-specific or population-specific tuning. We measured cancer detection (area under the ROC curve of the predicted cancer tissue fraction), all-slide ISUP agreement of the deployed detect-then-grade pipeline (quadratic-weighted kappa, QWK), and grading agreement on pathologist-confirmed cancers, at the slide level and, because a case carries up to two slides, at the patient level. The reference reader was S.A.; thresholds and operating points were cross-validated leave-one-out; scanners were compared by paired within-biopsy bootstrap and confidence intervals confirmed by patient-cluster bootstrap. Results: Detection was statistically equivalent across scanners (AUC 0.987 to 0.991; paired differences at most 0.003) and transferred to this non-Western cohort with no per-population tuning. At a 95% sensitivity operating point, the deployed pipeline reached cross-validated all-slide QWK of 0.86, 0.81, and 0.86 (Grundium, Hamamatsu, Leica), matching the inter-pathologist ceiling of 0.81, against 0.23 to 0.62 for the ungated model. Grading of confirmed cancers was scanner-dependent: the compact Grundium (0.63) did not differ from the clinical Leica (0.67; paired difference 0.04, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.11), while both exceeded Hamamatsu (0.44). Results held at the patient level, with grading somewhat lower for two scanners; the two slides of a case disagreed in grade in 43% of cases, and patient clustering did not widen the intervals. Conclusions: Cancer tissue fraction is a triage signal robust across scanner and transferable to an underrepresented population for detection, while grading is the scanner-sensitive step. Prostate grading models should be deployed as a detect-then-grade pipeline, with grading validated per device and confirmed on the local population.

documents.abstract: Malaysia’s service industry is undergoing simultaneous artificial-intelligence transformation and statutory minimum-wage pressure, creating a context in which service leaders are expected to show individualized care while also enforcing stronger productivity discipline. Drawing on conservation of resources theory and employee voice research, this three-wave, multi-source study examined whether the benevolent-authoritarian duality of paternalistic leadership was associated with promotive and prohibitive voice through ambivalent psychological safety and emotional resource depletion, and whether surface acting conditioned this pattern. The analytic sample comprised 360 service employee-supervisor dyads nested within 72 supervisors and 18 organizations/branches. Employees reported paternalistic leadership and surface acting at Time 1 and ambivalent psychological safety and emotional resource depletion at Time 2; supervisors rated promotive and prohibitive voice at Time 3. The benevolence x authoritarianism interaction was positively associated with ambivalent psychological safety (b = 0.400, p < 0.001), which was positively associated with emotional resource depletion (b = 0.390, p < 0.001). Surface acting strengthened the ambivalent-safety-to-depletion association (b = 0.151, p = 0.001). Resource depletion was negatively associated with promotive voice (b = −0.442, p < 0.001) and prohibitive voice (b = −0.247, p < 0.001), with a stronger association for promotive voice. Conditional indirect associations were stronger under high surface acting. These observational findings are consistent with the proposition that care-control leadership can reassure employees while being associated with lower emotional resources for constructive voice in AI- and wage-pressure service contexts.

Harmonic extension with its induced mass gives the classical Guyan approximation of graph Laplacian eigenvalues, and its leading error coefficient is a killed-Green quadratic form. We quantify how first hitting times govern this coefficient. For graphs assembled from cells with one retained vertex each, the Green form is compared with a retained-trace-weighted cell mean of the hitting potential to the retained set. The error is explicitly O(sqrt(mu)), where mu is the harmonic Rayleigh quotient, with constants determined by Dirichlet pinning, conductance bounds, crossing multiplicities, path lengths and congestion, uniformly in the number and sizes of the cells. A two-vertex-cell family shows that this order is sharp for general traces. Together with the condensed spectrum and one Poisson solve, the comparison gives computable same-index eigenvalue enclosures; a principal variant replaces modal Green solves by an inverse gap and a reverse Schwarz bound. On connected weighted finite-range periodic graphs with one retained type, Schur elimination and Bloch analyticity identify the coefficient of all ordered low eigenvalues on finite tori with the uniform mean hitting time, up to O(lambda). A six-vertex cell has mean one and an exact anisotropic correction. For its self-similar assembly, an interface tail proves a mean limit, which exact integer residual checks enclose in [1.50318,1.50837]; identifying the spectral coefficient with this limit still requires inverse-gap and mode-weighting estimates. Status and files: Version 1.0 of the focused manuscript Cell averages of hitting times in harmonic graph condensation, 20 pages with 41 references, prepared for submission to Linear Algebra and its Applications. This record includes the public manuscript PDF, its LaTeX source, and the complete verification archive with scripts, numerical records and exact integer mean witnesses. Detailed postal contact information is omitted from the public files. The original broader FDCL Part II working paper is at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23227296; proof and certification methodology is documented in FDCL Part IX v1.1 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23340664. AI use: OpenAI ChatGPT and Codex and Anthropic Claude assisted mathematical arguments, code, numerical analysis, literature comparison, and drafting and revision. Bin Seol directed the experiments and stress tests, co-developed verification methods, managed the data and evolving definitions, and selected, reviewed and revised the final claims. Bin Seol is the sole human author and accepts responsibility for the content. Finite floating-point spectral observations are distinguished from exact rational and stored integer residual checks; they are not formal machine verification.

documents.abstract: Abstract This paper examines whether students’ agent-related social perceptions of ChatGPT are associated with the perceived credibility of its feedback in academic tasks and whether such credibility, in turn, is related to students’ perceived learning. It also investigates whether the relationship between feedback credibility and perceived learning varies according to students’ sensitivity to the quality of their academic work and their sensitivity to grade-based rewards. To address this, we develop a theoretical model grounded in social perception theory and prior research on students’ experiences with AI-based tools. The model is tested using Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) on data collected from 230 students who completed an academic writing task. The findings reveal that students’ agent-related social perceptions—particularly perceived competence and human-like empathy—are positively connected to the credibility students attribute to its feedback. In turn, perceived feedback credibility is interestingly related to students’ perceived learning in the context of academic writing. Furthermore, the positive link between credibility and perceived learning is weaker among students with higher grade-based reward sensitivity. This research contributes to the educational technology literature by advancing understanding of how students evaluate the credibility of ChatGPT-generated feedback and how such evaluations are associated with learning perceptions. It also shows that agent-related social perceptions play a significant role in students’ credibility judgements. Finally, the findings offer practical implications for educators and students seeking to integrate ChatGPT effectively into academic activities.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This chapter introduces three prominent large language models (LLMs): Claude 4.6 (the latest version from Anthropic, as this book goes to print), Perplexity, and Grok. This chapter begins with a detailed discussion of Claude 4, describing it as an advanced, safety-focused model developed with Constitutional AI principles to ensure helpful, harmless, and honest responses. It highlights Claude’s core strengths—strong reasoning, coding proficiency, creative writing, analytical thinking, multi-language support, and the ability to create and maintain persistent “artifacts” (interactive code, documents, and diagrams). This chapter also notes Claude’s competitive advantages in nuanced reasoning, transparency about limitations, and ethical decision-making, while acknowledging potential weaknesses such as occasional hallucinations and limited third-party integrations. This chapter then covers Perplexity, emphasizing its real-time web search integration, citation accuracy, and strengths in research-oriented tasks, while noting limitations in creative writing and occasional latency under heavy load. Python code samples demonstrate how to interact with the Perplexity API and compare its features with other LLMs. The Grok section discusses its design philosophy (built by xAI, focused on truth-seeking and humor), strengths (uncensored responses, real-time knowledge via X integration), and weaknesses (potential bias and inconsistent performance), along with practical use cases. This chapter underscores how these models complement each other in different workflows. The final section of this chapter explores how these LLMs (particularly Claude, Perplexity, and Grok) can generate Python/Matplotlib code from natural-language prompts to create artistic and mathematical graphics based on polar equations (Archimedean spiral, Cardioid, Cochleoid, Conchoid, and Lituus). No prior knowledge of polar equations is required, as the models produce complete, runnable code. Each example includes explanations and placeholders for figures (e.g., Buckingham Palace, landscapes, Colosseum, and Space Needle). This chapter concludes by reinforcing the versatility of these LLMs in both practical programming and creative visualization tasks, positioning them as powerful tools for developers, researchers, and educators.

Introduction Digitized archives and health records offer growing opportunities for research, but approaches to extracting unstructured data remain heterogeneous. Large language models (LLMs) and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may facilitate extraction and synthesis, yet reporting guidance remains limited. This study develops CLEAR-Arch, a preliminary framework for transparent and reproducible reporting of LLM-assisted research. Method A scoping review–informed conceptual synthesis identified methodological and reporting considerations relevant to AI-assisted extraction, archival research, health informatics, and evidence synthesis. Candidate items were consolidated into reporting domains and used to develop performance indicators and a preliminary checklist. Results CLEAR-Arch proposes domains covering model specification, prompt design, document processing, extraction procedures, human validation, auditability, and data governance. Candidate indicators include precision, recall, F1-score, contextual accuracy, temporal fidelity, source-groundedness, inter-coder reliability, cross-source consistency, validation accuracy, and auditability. Conclusions CLEAR-Arch provides a preliminary, literature-informed framework for improving transparency, reproducibility, and methodological rigour in LLM-assisted research. Its domains, indicators, and reporting items are provisional, not established standards. Empirical validation, stakeholder consultation, content-validity assessment, and formal consensus development are needed before it can be considered standardized reporting guidance.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The clinical adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical diagnostics is frequently justified by retrospective metrics of algorithmic accuracy (such as AUROC and sensitivity), under the implicit assumption that early disease detection naturally improves patient prognosis. However, the translation of algorithmic inference into tangible clinical benefit is not self-evident and carries substantial risks of overdiagnosis, lead-time bias, false reassurance, and costly diagnostic cascades. This paper provides an epistemological and evidence-based analysis of AI-assisted diagnosis across five major clinical domains: oncology, neurodegeneration (Alzheimer’s disease), sepsis, acute ischemic stroke, and cardiovascular diseases. Drawing on seminal prospective and randomized clinical trials—including MASAI, GOLDEN BRIDGE II, EAGLE, and multi-site sepsis evaluations (TREWS, Epic Sepsis Model)—we demonstrate that diagnostic AI cannot be evaluated through a single universal benchmark. Instead, clinical utility depends heavily on disease-specific temporal horizons, confirmatory testing capacity, and actionable downstream care pathways. Furthermore, we differentiate metrological calibration (physical measurement traceability) from statistical calibration and GUM-defined measurement uncertainty, highlighting the critical role of data quality and reporting frameworks (TRIPOD+AI, DECIDE-AI, CONSORT-AI). Finally, we examine the human-AI interaction dyad, full lifecycle health economics, ethical-legal accountability, and health equity challenges in national contexts such as Türkiye. We conclude that the ultimate justification for medical AI is not to proliferate pathology labels, but to reliably alter clinical pathways and reduce preventable patient harm.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence demands unprecedented speed and capacity in data communication and computing, placing stringent requirements on electro‐optic modulators—the critical components for high‐speed optical interconnects. Conventional silicon photonic modulators, limited by the plasma dispersion mechanism, struggle to meet the needs of next‐generation high‐speed, low‐power systems. While thin‐film lithium niobate offers superior electro‐optic properties, its reliance on complex wafer bonding hinders fabrication efficiency, cost‐effectiveness, and compatibility with standard CMOS processes. Here, we demonstrate a promising approach: the first design and experimental realization of a Mach–Zehnder electro‐optic modulator monolithically integrating strontium barium niobate (SBN) thin films with silicon waveguides. The SBN film exhibits a large electro‐optic coefficient ( r 33 = 145 pm/V), several times greater than that of lithium niobate. The fabricated device achieves a half‐wave voltage–length product of 2.3 V·cm. Crucially, the SBN film can be preferentially grown directly atop silicon waveguides via magnetron sputtering, eliminating the need for wafer bonding. This synergistic innovation in material and fabrication greatly simplifies the process flow, enhances compatibility with silicon photonics, and offers a viable pathway toward scalable, low‐cost photonic integrated circuits for future optical communication and computing systems.

Introduction Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is widely expected to improve transparency and support appropriate human reliance on AI-assisted decision-making. However, the psychological processes through which explainability relates to reliance remain insufficiently understood, and explainability, transparency, and trust have largely been examined separately. Objectives This study develops and tests a psychological model of cognitive transparency in which AI explainability, algorithmic transparency, and perceived AI accuracy are associated with human reliance on AI through cognitive understanding, cognitive trust, and trust calibration, with AI literacy as a boundary condition. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 342 AI users in South Korea in May and June 2026. Each participant evaluated one self-selected AI system that they had personally used; all constructs were measured by self-report. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Results AI explainability (β = 0.349) and algorithmic transparency (β = 0.297) were positively associated with cognitive understanding. Cognitive understanding (β = 0.388) and, more strongly, perceived AI accuracy (β = 0.492) were associated with cognitive trust. Cognitive trust was associated with trust calibration (β = 0.631), which was associated with human reliance on AI (β = 0.600). All hypothesized indirect effects were significant, and AI literacy strengthened the association between AI explainability and cognitive understanding (β = 0.192). The model explained 36%–54% of the variance in the endogenous constructs and showed medium predictive power. Conclusion The findings are consistent with a sequence in which explainable AI relates to reliance through users’ understanding and trust judgments. Because all constructs were self-reported and measured at a single point in time, the results describe associations among users’ perceptions rather than causal effects, independently verified calibration, or objectively appropriate reliance. The findings suggest that AI developers in domains such as healthcare, education, and finance, where calibrated reliance is critical, should pair user-facing explanations with information about system accuracy and with AI literacy support.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are widely implemented in higher education to manage academic and administrative questions but their effectiveness is rarely measured in terms of knowledge base quality. This paper compares four chatbot platforms implemented in a live university environment: Google Dialogflow (intent-based), Tidio and Chatbase (auto-crawling), and an in-house Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) model created with LangChain, FAISS, and Mistral-7B. Ten sample questions regarding admissions, fees, library, and hostel facilities were employed to assess response precision, latency, and deployment time. Findings indicate that the RAG chatbot delivered the notable precision (65%) using a vetted dataset, while Tidio (45%) and Chatbase (55%) facilitated quicker deployment but provided incomplete or inaccurate responses due to limited web ingestion. With a small success rate of 10%, Dialogflow significantly failed with limited intent training, highlighting how intent-based systems rely on domain exhaustion. Results illustrate that the quality of knowledge base outweighs platform sophistication in defining chatbot performance, providing practical advice for institutions of differential technical capacity. The research also abets international aims of Quality Education (SDG 4) and Innovation and Infrastructure (SDG 9) by illustrating how disciplined, retrieval-augmented methodologies can provide fair and scalable student services.

SAE Level 3 automated vehicles may require drivers to resume control after being engaged in non-driving-related tasks. This study examined wearable vibrotactile takeover requests (TORs) delivered through rings and gloves, compared with a seat-back vibration baseline. Forty licensed drivers completed a driving simulator study using a 5 × 2 × 2 mixed factorial design with device type, TOR structure, and information type as independent variables. In the two-step condition, an auditory pre-warning was followed by a vibrotactile TOR. Results showed that takeover time measured from vibrotactile TOR onset was shorter in the two-step condition than in the single-step condition. No significant main effects of device type or information type on takeover time were observed. For subjective measures, the effect of TOR structure on workload depended on information type. The two-glove and two-ring configurations received the highest mean usefulness ratings, while glove-based configurations received the highest mean satisfaction ratings. Findings support wearable vibrotactile TORs as feasible alternatives for takeover support in automated driving.

University students face a rising prevalence of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and suicidal ideation that exceeds the capacity of conventional, resource-constrained campus support services. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted screening tools have emerged, many have evaluated selected modalities or isolated prediction tasks, and their integration with prospectively evaluated intervention pathways remains limited. This protocol describes the Comprehensive Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Mental Health Program for University Students in China (CAMPUS), a multi-center research program comprising a five-year prospective cohort, eight planned embedded randomized controlled trials, and exploratory multimodal AI and multi-omics studies across seven Chinese universities. Longitudinal cohort enrolment commenced at Henan Medical University in September 2025 and is planned to expand across seven participating universities. Multidimensional screening integrates psychological self-report (PHQ-9, GAD-7, ISI, BSI-CV, and others), physiological measurements (EEG, MRI, fNIRS, HRV, eye tracking, facial-expression analysis, ERP, voice acoustics), and an exploratory biospecimen component for multi-omics profiling, potentially including genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and microbiome analyses, subject to the finalization and approval of layer-specific protocols. Students identified through cohort screening as potentially eligible for an intervention trial will undergo trial-specific eligibility assessment. Those who meet the eligibility criteria and provide trial-specific informed consent will be individually randomized in a 1:1 ratio to the intervention or its comparator within one of eight separate two-arm, multi-center, parallel-group randomized controlled trials. A Transformer-based multimodal AI framework with SHAP-based feature attribution will be developed and internally evaluated for questionnaire-defined risk stratification and exploratory treatment-response prediction. The initial Henan Medical University cohort recruitment and university-student mental-health assessment were approved by the Ethics Review Committee of Henan Medical University (XYLL-20250484), and written informed consent is obtained from participants before enrolment. Each additional participating center will obtain local ethics approval before study activation. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, scientific conferences, and policy briefs, providing evidence that may inform the design and prospective evaluation of youth mental-health programs in other university settings. Clinical trial registration The two clinical trials were registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR). The registration details and URLs are as follows: ChiCTR2500113527: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=298271 ; ChiCTR2500113613: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=298268 .

documents.abstract: Soil settlement under loading is an important geotechnical problem that can affect the performance of foundations and structures. This thesis proposes a method that combines computer vision and machine learning to assess soil-surface displacement in laboratory tests. Sequential images are captured during staged loading, reference points are tracked, and calibrated image coordinates are converted into physical displacement. A regression model may then relate settlement estimates to applied pressure, moisture content, void ratio, specimen thickness and elapsed time. Model performance can be evaluated using independent displacement measurements and the root mean square error metric. This contribution is a proposed methodology rather than a report of completed experiments; no measured results are presented.

The digitalization of legal practice has expanded opportunities for communication, document management and legal research, while also increasing risks of unauthorized access to confidential information. This paper examines attorney–client confidentiality as a condition for the effective exercise of the right to qualified legal assistance and the protection of human rights. Drawing on Uzbekistan's constitutional and legislative framework, it analyses challenges related to electronic storage, cloud services, digital devices and artificial intelligence. It proposes a doctrinal model termed "digital immunity of a lawyer", understood as a combination of legal, procedural-organizational and technical safeguards. The paper argues that this concept should not mean absolute immunity from lawful procedural measures; rather, it should support lawful, proportionate and controlled access to digital information while protecting materials covered by professional confidentiality. It also emphasizes the need to preserve the lawyer's professional judgment and responsibility when using artificial intelligence.

Artificial intelligence is part of the human-built technosphere. The technosphere is the global system of machines, structures, and supply chains. It depends on the biosphere, and it competes with species and systems of the biosphere for energy, water, land, and materials. The biosphere is already outside its safe operating space. Seven of nine planetary boundaries have been crossed. Human use of the energy fixed by plants on land is near three times natural productivity. AI now helps draft, rank, and screen decisions in farming, energy, land use, water, and conservation. It also adds a fast-growing resource load of its own. This paper argues that AI used for biosphere-relevant decisions should not decide ecological hard limits by reading free text. Training on human preferences shapes ordinary behavior but does not encode ecological limits. Refusals that rest on a model reading prose can fail when the request is reworded. The paper presents Biosphere Sentinel, a reference design. In it, a language model may draft advice and fill an action form. A separate rule program outside the model then decides hard limits on coded, governed fields and returns one of four outcomes. The paper reports what the project tested and what it did not. A base model given the full constitution as a prompt hedged on both adversarial hard-limit queries. A coded energy-source field, with non-certification for off-list entries, ended a free-text failure cycle. Wrong approvals were zero across eight reference cases, and 161 locked checks passed. The decisive test, whether a language model can fill the coded fields dependably, was designed but not run. The paper records the peer review that led to withdrawal, the reasons the project was halted, the governance hazards any such design carries, and the conditions under which the work could resume.

documents.abstract: Digital materials are increasingly prevalent as a means of record creation. This paper presents interim results from the research project “Long-term preservation of the authenticity of digital originals using blockchain technology and artificial intelligence (I.Trust.Original)”, funded by the European Union’s NextGenerationEU fund, and focuses on concepts and tools for archiving digital materials. The authors review the concepts of the digital original and the archival bond and examine their application within the Open Archival Information System (OAIS) framework. Blockchain and distributed ledger technologies (DLT) are analysed as mechanisms for creating digital originals and for ensuring integrity, transparency, and trust. The paper also explores the role of artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models (LLMs), in archival processes and in supporting blockchain-based preservation. Semantic web and linked data are regarded as tools for enhancing interoperability and discoverability, while smart contracts are recognised in the context of rights management. The paper aims to map these concepts and technologies and assess their impact on the archiving of digital originals, highlighting key benefits and limitations. It emphasises the interconnectedness of archival theory and technological innovation, and outlines directions for future research and practical implementation.

In onboard environments characterised by high operational risk, near-miss reporting is an important mechanism for identifying latent risks, preventing accidents and supporting organisational improvement. However, there remains limited empirical understanding of whether the just culture advocated in formal systems can be translated into the lived reporting experience of seafarers who are willing, able and motivated to report near-miss incidents on a sustained basis. To address this issue, this study draws on semi-structured interviews with seafarers and shore-based managers. Six interrelated themes are identified: ease of reporting, motivation to report, trust, reporting independence, feedback and acknowledgement. The findings indicate that near-miss reporting is more likely to occur in organisational contexts where reporting is accessible, safe and worthwhile. Complicated procedures, paperwork burdens and hierarchical pressure weaken seafarers’ willingness to report, whereas simplified procedures, fair management, low exposure communication channels, timely feedback and positive acknowledgement help strengthen reporting willingness and promote experience sharing. This study provides context-specific empirical evidence on how formal just culture is translated into frontline reporting practice and offers practical insights that may inform efforts to improve near-miss reporting, reduce reporting concerns and strengthen closed-loop feedback in comparable organisational or cultural settings.
